options.a: The listing broker is owed a commission unless the seller personally finds the buyer during the term
options.b: The seller may list with several brokers and pays a commission only to the broker who procures the buyer
options.c: The listing broker is owed a commission if the property sells during the term, regardless of who finds the buyer
options.d: The broker keeps any sale proceeds above the seller's stated minimum price as the commission

distractorExplanations.a: That describes an exclusive agency listing, where the seller keeps the right to sell without owing a commission.
distractorExplanations.b: That describes an open listing, where only the procuring broker is paid and the seller may also sell directly.
distractorExplanations.d: That describes a net listing, which concerns how the commission is calculated, not exclusivity of the right to sell.

california-real-estate-readiness-check-c.explanation: Exclusive right-to-sell typically protects the listing broker's commission if a sale occurs during the listing term. The exact protection follows the terms of the listing agreement.

options.a: Known latent defects or conditions that could significantly affect value or desirability
options.b: The seller's reasons for selling and the lowest price the seller is willing to accept
options.c: The racial or religious makeup of the neighborhood surrounding the property
options.d: That a former occupant of the home was living with HIV or AIDS

distractorExplanations.b: Seller motivation and bottom-line price are confidential client information, not material property facts.
distractorExplanations.c: Discussing neighborhood racial or religious composition is steering under the Fair Housing Act, not a required disclosure.
distractorExplanations.d: HIV/AIDS is a protected disability under federal fair housing law; it is not a material property fact to disclose.

california-real-estate-readiness-check-c.explanation: Material property defects and legally required disclosures must be shared; confidential motivations may be protected. Disclosure duties follow applicable law.

options.a: Suggest an offer amount, since helping the buyer also helps close the sale
options.b: Avoid acting as the buyer's advocate and stay within the listing agency role
options.c: Share the seller's lowest acceptable price so the buyer can offer efficiently
options.d: Give a price opinion as long as the buyer has signed the agency disclosure form

distractorExplanations.a: Recommending an offer amount is buyer advocacy that conflicts with the listing agent's loyalty to the seller.
distractorExplanations.c: Revealing the seller's bottom line breaches the confidentiality duty owed to the seller client.
distractorExplanations.d: Signing an agency disclosure does not create buyer representation; the agent still represents only the seller.

california-real-estate-readiness-check-c.explanation: Listing agents represent the seller; advocacy for a buyer requires a proper agency shift/disclosure. If allowed, the brokerage may properly create buyer agency with required disclosures.

options.a: Inheritance
options.b: Homestead
options.c: Reversion
options.d: Survivorship

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses joint tenancy with tenancy in common; a joint tenant's interest passes to co-owners, not heirs.
distractorExplanations.b: Homestead is a separate protection of a residence from certain creditors, not a feature of joint tenancy.
distractorExplanations.c: Reversion is the grantor's future interest after a life estate, unrelated to co-ownership rights.

options.a: Public use and the owner's written consent
options.b: Just compensation set by the county assessor
options.c: Public use/purpose and just compensation
options.d: A court finding that the owner is delinquent on taxes

distractorExplanations.a: Eminent domain is the government's power to take without consent; only just compensation is owed to the owner.
distractorExplanations.b: Compensation is fair market value set by negotiation or the court, not the assessor's tax value; public use is also required.
distractorExplanations.d: Tax delinquency leads to a tax sale, a different process; eminent domain needs public use and compensation.

california-real-estate-readiness-check-c.explanation: Takings require public purpose and just compensation under the Constitution. This framework comes from the Fifth Amendment.

options.a: Obtain the highest possible price even when the seller directs a quicker sale
options.b: Promote the seller's interests with loyalty, care, and obedience within the law
options.c: Treat buyer and seller with equal advocacy so both receive fair representation
options.d: Advise the seller on title and tax matters as the seller's legal representative

distractorExplanations.a: Price is not the top duty; obedience requires following the seller's lawful instruction to favor a quick sale.
distractorExplanations.c: Equal advocacy describes a neutral or dual role; a listing broker owes loyalty to the seller client, not both sides.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses agency with legal practice; a broker must refer title and tax questions to an attorney or CPA.

options.a: The buyer's down payment, which the lender holds until the loan closes
options.b: Consideration required to make a purchase contract valid and binding
options.c: A deposit the listing broker may treat as commission once the offer is accepted
options.d: A good-faith deposit typically held in escrow/trust pending contract performance

distractorExplanations.a: Earnest money is usually credited toward the down payment but is held by the broker or escrow, not the lender.
distractorExplanations.b: Mutual promises are sufficient consideration; earnest money is not legally required for a valid contract.
distractorExplanations.c: Earnest money stays in trust until closing or release; applying it to commission early is conversion.

options.a: The buyer is credited; it reduces cash needed
options.b: The item is split evenly between buyer and seller
options.c: The buyer is charged; it increases cash needed
options.d: The lender pays it; it reduces the loan amount

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the entries: a credit reduces what the buyer owes, while a debit is a charge to the buyer.
distractorExplanations.b: Splits are prorations or negotiated sharing, shown as separate debits to each party, not the meaning of a debit.
distractorExplanations.d: A buyer debit is a charge to the buyer; lender-paid items appear as credits, and the loan amount is unchanged.

california-real-estate-readiness-check-c.explanation: Debits charge a party; buyer debits typically increase funds due at closing. For the seller, a debit reduces sale proceeds.

options.a: Complete CE only for the first renewal, then no further hours
options.b: Complete required CE hours and topics before renewal
options.c: Complete CE hours after renewal, during the next license period
options.d: Pay a late renewal fee in place of the CE hours

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the first-renewal course package with later renewals; California requires CE for every four-year renewal, not just once.
distractorExplanations.c: Reverses the timing: CE must be finished before the renewal application is filed, not made up during the following license term.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the late-renewal fee with the education requirement; paying a fee does not substitute for completing the required CE hours.

options.a: Negotiate price and terms with buyers as long as the broker reviews the final contract
options.b: Show properties to prospective buyers and answer their questions about value when the agent is unavailable
options.c: Perform administrative tasks that do not require a license (with broker supervision limits)
options.d: Sign listing agreements on the broker's behalf if given written authority by the broker

distractorExplanations.a: Broker review does not cure the problem: negotiating price or terms with the public is licensed activity an unlicensed assistant cannot perform.
distractorExplanations.b: Showing property and discussing value with prospects is licensed activity under DRE guidance; an unlicensed assistant is limited to clerical support.
distractorExplanations.d: Written authority from the broker does not let an unlicensed person execute listing agreements; taking listings requires a DRE license.

options.a: Directing buyers toward or away from neighborhoods based on a protected class
options.b: Refusing to make loans in an area because of the racial makeup of its residents
options.c: Using ads that state a preference for buyers of one protected class
options.d: Inducing owners to sell by suggesting protected-class entry will lower values

distractorExplanations.a: Describes steering, which channels buyers by protected class; blockbusting targets owners with panic-selling warnings about neighborhood change.
distractorExplanations.b: Describes redlining, a lending practice of denying credit by area; blockbusting is a sales-solicitation tactic aimed at property owners.
distractorExplanations.c: Describes discriminatory advertising, a separate Fair Housing Act violation; blockbusting is soliciting sales by predicting neighborhood change.

california-real-estate-readiness-check-c.explanation: Blockbusting is a prohibited panic-selling tactic under fair housing law. It is an illegal fair housing practice (also called panic peddling).

options.a: Reasonable supervision of the licensed activities of employed salespersons
options.b: Supervision only of salespersons in their first two years of licensure
options.c: Supervision of client trust funds, with salespersons responsible for their own conduct
options.d: Reviewing salesperson files after a consumer complaint triggers a DRE audit

distractorExplanations.b: Invents a probationary window; the California broker's supervision duty covers every employed salesperson, not just new licensees.
distractorExplanations.c: Trust-fund handling is part of the duty, but the broker also remains responsible for supervising salespersons' licensed activities, not just money.
distractorExplanations.d: Reactive review is not reasonable supervision; California requires ongoing policies and oversight of salesperson activity, not complaint-driven checks.

options.a: Earthquake fault zones that trigger disclosure and development restrictions
options.b: Coastal zone permits required by the Coastal Commission for shoreline building
options.c: Seismic hazard zones for liquefaction and landslides mapped under a later act
options.d: Very high fire hazard severity zones that require defensible-space disclosure

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses Alquist-Priolo with the California Coastal Act, which governs coastal-zone development permits, not fault-rupture zones.
distractorExplanations.c: Describes the Seismic Hazards Mapping Act (liquefaction and landslide zones); Alquist-Priolo specifically maps surface fault-rupture zones.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses Alquist-Priolo with fire hazard severity zone disclosures, which concern wildfire risk rather than active earthquake faults.

options.a: Accept a signed "as-is" clause in place of the TDS, since it waives disclosure
options.b: Let the buyer's home inspection report stand in for the seller's TDS disclosure
options.c: Not ignore the requirement — advise that the statutory disclosure obligation still applies
options.d: Complete the seller's section of the TDS personally, based on the agent's own visual inspection

distractorExplanations.a: An as-is sale does not waive the California TDS; the seller must still disclose known material defects in covered transfers.
distractorExplanations.b: A buyer's inspection report is not a substitute; the statutory TDS is the seller's own disclosure of known property conditions.
distractorExplanations.d: The agent's visual-inspection section supplements but cannot replace the seller's own disclosures; the agent may not fill in the seller's part.

california-real-estate-readiness-check-c.explanation: Agents cannot waive statutory seller disclosure duties; they must counsel compliance and avoid misrepresentation. The agent should escalate appropriately (broker, counsel) rather than proceed without the required disclosure.

options.a: Ads must show the licensee's name and DRE number, but not the employing broker
options.b: Ads generally must disclose licensee identity/status and responsible broker information
options.c: Ads may use a team name by itself as long as every team member holds a license
options.d: Only the broker's name must appear in ads; salesperson names and license numbers are optional

distractorExplanations.a: Team and salesperson advertising must also identify the responsible broker; showing only the licensee's name and number is incomplete.
distractorExplanations.c: A team name alone is not enough; California requires the responsible broker's identity to appear with the team name in advertising.
distractorExplanations.d: Reverses the rule: California requires the salesperson's name and DRE license number on solicitation materials, not just the broker's name.

options.a: Commercial deals involve sophisticated parties, so licensees owe no disclosure duties and fiduciary duties can be waived orally
options.b: Commercial deals focus on income and leases, so the DRE license law does not apply and a separate commercial broker license is required instead
options.c: Commercial deals may involve income analysis, leases, environmental issues, and sophisticated parties but still require disclosure and honesty
options.d: Commercial deals use the same TDS and residential disclosure forms as one-to-four unit homes, with value based on comparable sales

distractorExplanations.a: Sophisticated parties do not remove license-law duties; California licensees in commercial deals still owe honesty, disclosure, and fiduciary duties.
distractorExplanations.b: California has no separate commercial license; the same DRE broker or salesperson license covers commercial brokerage and the license law applies.
distractorExplanations.d: The TDS covers one-to-four unit residential transfers; commercial value relies mainly on income capitalization, not residential-style comparable sales.

options.a: California agency form for residential sales confirming which agency relationships exist in the deal
options.b: California natural hazard disclosure form identifying flood, fire, and earthquake fault zones affecting a property
options.c: California lender form for residential loans estimating the buyer's closing costs and loan terms
options.d: California seller disclosure form for many residential transfers identifying known property condition issues

distractorExplanations.a: Describes the agency disclosure and confirmation forms; the TDS is the seller's statement of known property condition issues.
distractorExplanations.b: Describes the Natural Hazard Disclosure (NHD) statement, which reports mapped hazard zones; the TDS covers the seller's known condition issues.
distractorExplanations.c: Describes the federal Loan Estimate under TRID, a lender cost disclosure, not a California seller property-condition form.

options.a: A cooperating broker who works with the buyer and owes fiduciary duties to that buyer
options.b: A broker/agent assists another agent and owes fiduciary duties to the original principal
options.c: A broker who refers a client to another brokerage for a referral fee and then has no further duties
options.d: One broker represents both buyer and seller in the same transaction with written consent

distractorExplanations.a: Describes a buyer's agent; a subagent works through the listing broker and owes fiduciary duties to the seller, the original principal.
distractorExplanations.c: Describes a referral arrangement; a subagent actively assists in the transaction and owes the original principal full fiduciary duties.
distractorExplanations.d: Describes dual agency, where one broker represents both parties; subagency extends the listing broker's agency to a cooperating broker.

options.a: Full fiduciary duties of loyalty and confidentiality owed equally to both the seller and the buyer
options.b: No duties to the buyer at all, because the buyer is not the agent's client
options.c: Honesty, fair dealing, and disclosure of known material facts, but fiduciary duties to seller.
options.d: Disclosure of material facts when the buyer asks in writing, with fiduciary duties to seller

distractorExplanations.a: That describes dual agency with consent; a seller's agent owes the buyer honesty and disclosure but fiduciary loyalty to the seller.
distractorExplanations.b: California imposes duties on a seller's agent toward the buyer too: honest and fair dealing and disclosure of known material facts affecting value.
distractorExplanations.d: The duty to disclose known material facts is affirmative in California; it does not depend on the buyer asking or requesting in writing.

options.a: Different licensees within one brokerage may work with different parties, which eliminates any dual agency at the broker level as a matter of law
options.b: One licensee represents both buyer and seller in a transaction after both parties give informed written consent
options.c: A licensee from another brokerage is designated by the listing broker as a subagent to represent the seller
options.d: Different licensees within a brokerage may work with different parties, but broker-level dual agency can still exist depending on law

distractorExplanations.a: Assigning separate licensees does not erase broker-level dual agency; in California the broker remains a dual agent when both sides are in-house.
distractorExplanations.b: Describes single-licensee dual agency; designated agency assigns different licensees in the same brokerage to each party.
distractorExplanations.c: Describes subagency across firms; designated agency concerns separate licensees within the same brokerage serving different parties.

options.a: An estate that lasts for the owner's lifetime and then passes to a named remainderman, subject to government powers
options.b: Ownership that reverts to the grantor if a stated condition in the deed is broken, such as a restriction on use
options.c: The greatest private ownership estate, inheritable and freely transferable, subject to government powers and private restrictions
options.d: A right to possess and use the property for a fixed term under a written lease, freely assignable to others unless the lease restricts it

distractorExplanations.a: Describes a life estate, which ends at the death of the measuring life; fee simple absolute is inheritable with no time limit.
distractorExplanations.b: Describes a fee simple defeasible (qualified fee), which can end on a stated condition; fee simple absolute carries no such condition.
distractorExplanations.d: Describes a leasehold (estate for years), a nonfreehold interest; fee simple absolute is the highest freehold ownership estate.

options.a: A leasehold estate giving possession for a fixed term of years
options.b: The most complete ownership interest recognized in real property
options.c: A freehold estate that lasts only for the life of a named person
options.d: An ownership interest that ends if a stated condition is violated

distractorExplanations.a: A leasehold (estate for years) is a nonfreehold possessory interest; fee simple absolute is the fullest freehold ownership.
distractorExplanations.c: Describes a life estate, which ends at the measuring life's death; fee simple absolute is inheritable without a time limit.
distractorExplanations.d: Describes a fee simple defeasible, which can terminate on a condition; fee simple absolute has no such limitation.

options.a: Unequal shares
options.b: Survivorship
options.c: Devise by will
options.d: Homestead exemption

distractorExplanations.a: Unequal shares are a tenancy-in-common feature; joint tenancy requires equal undivided interests (unity of interest).
distractorExplanations.c: A joint tenant cannot defeat survivorship by will; the interest passes to the surviving joint tenants, so devise is a TIC feature.
distractorExplanations.d: The homestead exemption protects equity from certain creditors under state law; it is not a feature of joint tenancy title.

options.a: A leasehold estate giving possession for a fixed term of years
options.b: A freehold estate that lasts only for the life of a named person
options.c: An ownership interest that ends if a stated condition is violated
options.d: The most complete ownership interest recognized in real property

distractorExplanations.a: A leasehold (estate for years) is a nonfreehold possessory interest; fee simple absolute is the fullest freehold ownership.
distractorExplanations.b: Describes a life estate, which ends at the measuring life's death; fee simple absolute is inheritable without a time limit.
distractorExplanations.c: Describes a fee simple defeasible, which can terminate on a condition; fee simple absolute has no such limitation.

options.a: Promote the seller's interests with loyalty, care, and obedience within the law
options.b: Obtain the highest possible price even when the seller instructs a quicker sale
options.c: Represent both parties equally once the buyer signs a purchase agreement
options.d: Disclose the seller's lowest acceptable price to buyers to speed negotiations

distractorExplanations.b: Obedience to lawful instructions outranks the agent's own price goal; a seller may prioritize speed or terms over top price.
distractorExplanations.c: Equal representation of both sides is dual agency and requires disclosure and consent; signing an offer does not create it.
distractorExplanations.d: Revealing the seller's bottom line breaches the duties of loyalty and confidentiality owed to the seller client.

options.a: At closing, when the final settlement statement is reviewed and signed by both parties
options.b: Before or as soon as practicable when the dual/designated relationship arises
options.c: When the first offer is drafted, even if the relationship began earlier
options.d: Within five days after the purchase contract is accepted by the seller

distractorExplanations.a: Disclosure at closing is too late; consent must be informed before the dual or designated relationship affects negotiations.
distractorExplanations.c: Waiting until an offer is written is too late if the dual or designated relationship already arose at a showing or earlier.
distractorExplanations.d: Invents a post-acceptance grace period; disclosure comes before or as soon as practicable when the relationship arises, not after acceptance.

california-real-estate-readiness-check-c.explanation: Agency disclosure timing is early—when the dual or designated relationship is created or contemplated. Follow the applicable state agency-disclosure rules for the exact form and timing.

options.a: Later found a better price elsewhere
options.b: Signed without an earnest money deposit
options.c: Was induced by fraud or was a minor
options.d: Was adjudged incompetent before signing

distractorExplanations.a: Buyer's remorse or a better deal elsewhere is not a legal ground to avoid a contract; fraud or incapacity is.
distractorExplanations.b: Earnest money is not required for a valid contract; consideration can be the mutual promises, so its absence does not make it voidable.
distractorExplanations.d: A contract by someone already adjudged incompetent by a court is void, not voidable; voidable applies to minors and fraud victims.

california-real-estate-readiness-check-c.explanation: Fraud or lack of capacity can make a contract voidable by the protected party. Whether the contract is voidable depends on the circumstances (e.g., ratification after reaching majority).

options.a: An FHA loan is made with a 3.5% down payment
options.b: A VA loan is made with zero down payment to a veteran
options.c: Conventional LTV is low (commonly below 80%)
options.d: Conventional LTV is high (commonly above 80%)

distractorExplanations.a: FHA loans carry FHA mortgage insurance premiums (MIP), not private mortgage insurance; PMI is a conventional-loan product.
distractorExplanations.b: VA loans have no monthly mortgage insurance; the VA guaranty and funding fee take its place, so PMI does not apply.
distractorExplanations.c: Reverses the threshold; PMI is triggered when the conventional LTV exceeds 80%, and borrowers at or below 80% LTV usually avoid it.

options.a: Can adjust based on an index plus margin, subject to caps
options.b: Can adjust based on the margin alone, with the index fixed
options.c: Can adjust at the lender's discretion, with no caps
options.d: Is fixed for the loan term but payments can rise with taxes

distractorExplanations.b: Inverts the formula: the margin is the fixed part set at origination, while the index moves and drives rate changes.
distractorExplanations.c: ARM changes follow a published index under the note, and periodic and lifetime caps limit how far the rate can move.
distractorExplanations.d: Describes a fixed-rate loan with escrow changes; an ARM's interest rate itself resets periodically based on index plus margin.

options.a: Physical damage to the home from fire, flood, or other casualty
options.b: Covered title defects and claims against ownership per the policy
options.c: Losses to the lender if the borrower later defaults on the mortgage note
options.d: Defects and liens that arise after the policy date at closing

distractorExplanations.a: Casualty loss is covered by hazard (homeowner's) insurance; title insurance covers defects in title, not physical damage.
distractorExplanations.c: Default risk is covered by mortgage insurance (PMI/MIP); a lender's title policy protects the lien's validity and priority, not repayment.
distractorExplanations.d: Title policies look backward: they insure against covered defects existing at the policy date, not liens created afterward.

options.a: Originate purchase loans directly to borrowers at retail branches
options.b: Set the federal funds rate that drives mortgage interest rates
options.c: Insure lenders against borrower default on high-LTV conventional loans
options.d: Buy and sell existing mortgages, improving liquidity for originators

distractorExplanations.a: Origination happens in the primary mortgage market; the secondary market buys loans after they are made.
distractorExplanations.b: The Federal Reserve sets monetary policy and the federal funds rate; the secondary market buys and pools existing mortgages.
distractorExplanations.c: That is the role of private mortgage insurers; secondary-market entities such as Fannie Mae buy loans to supply liquidity.

options.a: Maximum interest rates that may be charged on certain loans
options.b: Minimum disclosures of loan costs such as the APR to borrowers
options.c: Kickbacks and referral fees among settlement service providers
options.d: Lending discrimination based on race, sex, or marital status

distractorExplanations.b: Cost disclosure such as APR is governed by the Truth in Lending Act (Regulation Z), not usury laws, which cap the interest rate.
distractorExplanations.c: Kickbacks and unearned referral fees are prohibited by RESPA Section 8; usury laws address maximum interest charges.
distractorExplanations.d: Credit discrimination is barred by the Equal Credit Opportunity Act; usury laws limit how much interest a lender may charge.

options.a: Fund construction in stages through draws, then convert to a permanent loan once the home is finished
options.b: Finance a short-term gap, often between purchase of a new home and sale of an existing one
options.c: Combine a first mortgage and a second loan to avoid PMI on a new home purchase
options.d: Refinance an existing home to lower the rate over a new 30-year amortizing term

distractorExplanations.a: Describes a construction-to-permanent loan with staged draws; a bridge loan is a short-term gap loan tied to a home sale.
distractorExplanations.c: Describes a piggyback (80-10-10) loan structure used to avoid PMI, not a temporary gap loan between two homes.
distractorExplanations.d: A rate-and-term refinance is long-term permanent financing; a bridge loan is short-term and repaid when the old home sells.

options.a: Both interest and principal so the unpaid balance declines to zero by maturity
options.b: Interest only for the term, with the full principal due as a balloon at maturity
options.c: Equal principal portions each month, so the interest portion stays level
options.d: Mostly principal in the early years and mostly interest near the end of the term

distractorExplanations.b: Describes an interest-only (term) loan with a balloon payment; a fully amortizing loan retires principal with each payment.
distractorExplanations.c: Reverses the mix: on a level payment, the interest portion falls and the principal portion grows over the life of the loan.
distractorExplanations.d: Backwards: early payments are mostly interest because the balance is highest; the principal share grows toward maturity.

options.a: Requiring APR disclosure and a right of rescission on certain refinance loans
options.b: Prohibiting lending discrimination based on race, religion, sex, or marital status
options.c: Requiring lenders to report mortgage application data by census tract to detect redlining patterns
options.d: Banning certain kickbacks and requiring settlement cost disclosures in covered transactions

distractorExplanations.a: APR disclosure and the right of rescission come from the Truth in Lending Act (Regulation Z), not RESPA's kickback and settlement rules.
distractorExplanations.b: Lending discrimination is barred by the Equal Credit Opportunity Act and Fair Housing Act; RESPA targets settlement costs and kickbacks.
distractorExplanations.c: Describes the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act (HMDA); RESPA bans kickbacks and requires settlement cost disclosures.

options.a: Requires extra payment if the borrower makes a payment more than 15 days late
options.b: Lets the borrower pay off early with no charge, when the note allows it
options.c: Requires extra payment if the borrower pays off early, when the note allows it
options.d: Lets the lender demand full payoff if the borrower sells the property

distractorExplanations.a: Describes a late charge triggered by a missed due date; a prepayment penalty applies when the loan is paid off ahead of schedule.
distractorExplanations.b: Describes a prepayment privilege (open) clause, the opposite of a penalty; a prepayment penalty adds a charge for early payoff.
distractorExplanations.d: Describes a due-on-sale (alienation) clause; a prepayment penalty is a charge for paying the loan off early.

options.a: An FHA loan is made with a 3.5% down payment
options.b: A VA loan is made with zero down payment to a veteran
options.c: Conventional LTV is low (commonly below 80%)
options.d: Conventional LTV is high (commonly above 80%)

distractorExplanations.a: FHA loans carry FHA mortgage insurance premiums (MIP), not private mortgage insurance; PMI is a conventional-loan product.
distractorExplanations.b: VA loans have no monthly mortgage insurance; the VA guaranty and funding fee take its place, so PMI does not apply.
distractorExplanations.c: Reverses the threshold; PMI is triggered when the conventional LTV exceeds 80%, and borrowers at or below 80% LTV usually avoid it.
